name: Nursing SBAR Handover & Escalation
description: Evaluates a nurse handing over or escalating a patient to another nurse or to a physician, using the Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation framework within the nursing scope of practice.

anchors.80-100: Clear, fluent, near-native phrasing; the receiving clinician never has to ask for a repeat.
anchors.50-70: Understandable but occasional hesitations or grammar errors slow the handover.
anchors.10-40: Frequent errors that impede understanding of a time-critical message.

anchors.80-100: Uses nursing and clinical terminology accurately; vitals, trends, and interventions are stated precisely.
anchors.50-70: Mostly accurate, but vague quantifiers ('a bit low', 'not great') replace the actual observation.
anchors.10-40: Misstates observations or terminology in ways that could mislead the receiving clinician.

anchors.80-100: Clearly articulates Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation, and opens by identifying self, unit, and patient.
anchors.50-70: Misses one component, or buries the reason for the call after a long background.
anchors.10-40: Missing multiple components or highly disorganized; the listener cannot tell what is being asked.

anchors.80-100: Conveys how sick the patient is in the first two sentences and states clearly how soon a response is needed.
anchors.50-70: Communicates the facts but leaves the urgency for the listener to infer.
anchors.10-40: Understates a deteriorating patient, or escalates without saying what response is needed and by when.

anchors.80-100: Respectful and concise; reads back or confirms the plan and any new orders before ending the call.
anchors.50-70: Mostly respectful but may get flustered, or ends without confirming what was agreed.
anchors.10-40: Defensive, apologetic to the point of obscuring the message, or verbose without getting to the point.

checklist.item: Identified self, role, unit, and the patient at the start
Stated the Situation — why this call is happening right now
Provided relevant Background (admission reason, relevant history, what has already been done)
Gave a clear Assessment, including objective observations (vitals, trends, exam findings)
Made a specific Recommendation or request within the nursing scope (come and review, give an order, escalate further)
Stated how urgently a response is needed
Read back or confirmed the plan, orders, or outstanding tasks before ending
